alternative: Give the entity one struct: embed both capability structs (each with its function-pointer table as first member) in a single object, and where a subsystem only needs to call back, register a function pointer with a void *ctx instead of creating a second object. Use a twin-shaped pair of structs only when two subsystems each require their own first-member base and their own allocation (a widget list plus a scheduler list); then keep ownership one-way, make the back-pointer non-owning, and define which side frees the pair.
idiom_name: two structs with embedded vtables and a mutual back-pointer (a hand-built re-implementation of a feature C never had)
implementation_notes: C has no inheritance, so the premise of the pattern - a class that cannot extend two parents - does not exist. Subtype compatibility is hand-built by making the base struct the first member of the derived struct (the rule that a pointer to a struct can be converted to a pointer to its first member is guaranteed by the standard, and this is the standard C emulation of single inheritance), and the technique is normally applied once per object, not twice. What replaces the twin pair: embed both capability structs in one object - each with its function-pointer table as its first member - and forward explicitly, or register a callback plus a void *ctx where a subsystem only needs to call back. The two-struct twin shape is worth writing only when two independent subsystems each demand their own object with their own first-member base and their own allocation (a widget tree plus a timer list); even then keep ownership one-way and the back-pointer in the non-owning struct.
pitfalls: C has no runtime type information and no ownership rules: the mutual pointer must be set by hand in a constructor function, and a stale back-pointer is an out-of-bounds access rather than an exception.
Two structs mean two allocations and two vtables to keep consistent; unless one owner is defined, the entity can be destroyed through one pointer while the other pointer still refers to it.
The base struct must be the first member for pointer casts to be valid - inserting any field before it silently breaks every upcast.
